etymologies.etymologyHTML: Via Middle English, borrowed from Old French rai, from Latin radius (“staff, stake, spoke”). Doublet of radius.

definitions.definition: A beam of light or radiation.

quote.citation: 1922, E[ric] R[ücker] Eddison, The Worm Ouroboros‎[1], London: Jonathan Cape, page 5:
quote.text: Strangely light and delicate was his frame and seeming, yet with a sense of slumbering power beneath, as the delicate peak of a snow mountain seen afar in the low red rays of morning.

definitions.definition: (zoology) A rib-like reinforcement of bone or cartilage in a fish's fin.
(zoology) One of the spheromeres of a radiate, especially one of the arms of a starfish or an ophiuran.
(botany) A radiating part of a flower or plant; the marginal florets of a compound flower, such as an aster or a sunflower; one of the pedicels of an umbel or other circular flower cluster; radius.
(obsolete) Sight; perception; vision; from an old theory of vision, that sight was something which proceeded from the eye to the object seen.

quote.citation: 1728, [Alexander Pope], “(please specify the page)”, in The Dunciad. An Heroic Poem. […], Dublin, London:  […]  A. Dodd, →OCLC:
quote.text: All eyes direct their rays / On him, and crowds turn coxcombs as they gaze.

definitions.definition: (mathematics) A line extending indefinitely in one direction from a point.
(transitive) To emit something as if in rays.

quote.citation: 1889, Robert Browning, letter to Dr. Furnivall:
quote.text: I had no particular woman in my mind; certainly never intended to personify wisdom, philosophy, or any other abstraction; and the orb, raying colour out of whiteness, was altogether a fancy of my own.

definitions.definition: (intransitive) To radiate as if in rays.

quote.citation: 1928, Archives of Pathology and Laboratory Medicine, page 219:
quote.text: Rats' eyes with ulcus serpens were successfully treated; one second of raying stopped the progress of the ulcer, which healed uninterruptedly.

etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English raye, rayȝe, from Old French raie, from Latin raia, of uncertain origin. Compare Middle English reyhhe, reihe, reȝge (“ray, skate”), from Old English reohhe (“ray”).

definitions.definition: A marine fish with a flat body, large wing-like fins, and a whip-like tail.
(obsolete) To stain or soil; to defile. [16th–19th c.]

quote.citation: 1596, Edmund Spenser, “Book VI, Canto IV”, in The Faerie Queene. […], London:  […]  [John Wolfe] for William Ponsonbie, →OCLC:
quote.text: From his soft eyes the teares he wypt away, / And from his face the filth that did it ray  […] .

quote.citation: 1596, Edmund Spenser, “Book V, Canto II”, in The Faerie Queene. […], London:  […]  [John Wolfe] for William Ponsonbie, →OCLC, stanza 50:
quote.text: spoyling all her geares and goodly ray

etymologies.etymologyHTML: From its sound, by analogy with the letters chay, jay, gay, kay, which it resembles graphically.

definitions.definition: The letter ⟨/⟩, one of two which represent the r sound in Pitman shorthand.
